52: ## Step 3: Campus Locations and Adjacency
53: * **Acceptance Criteria:** AC-17 to AC-20
54: * **What was built:**
55:   * Hierarchical location model (`campus_locations`) supporting 5 distinct levels (`campus`, `building`, `floor`, `room`, `area`), parent pointers, optional coordinates stored rounded to 3 decimal places (`NUMERIC(8, 3)`), and case-insensitive sibling uniqueness index `uq_locations_parent_name_ci`.
56:   * Symmetric building adjacency table (`location_adjacency`) linking adjacent buildings with distinct checks.
57:   * Tree hierarchy cycle detection preventing any node from becoming its own ancestor (HTTP 422 `cannot_become_own_ancestor`).
58:   * Administrative endpoints for tree CRUD, delete protection on in-use locations (HTTP 409), and adjacency pairing.
59:   * Pure domain location scoring function `calculate_location_score` in `backend/app/domain/location.py` [LEARN] implementing the exact scoring matrix: identical (1.0), ancestor (0.8), lowest common ancestor floor/area (0.7), building (0.6), adjacent buildings (0.5), same campus (0.2), different campus (0.0), and missing location (`null`).
60: * **Why it is designed that way:**
61:   * Physical campus environments feature multi-story buildings and indoor rooms where GPS signals degrade or lack vertical resolution; a discrete hierarchical tree paired with building adjacency reflects real-world proximity accurately.
62:   * Isolating `calculate_location_score` as a pure function with zero database or framework dependencies keeps mathematical scoring lightning-fast, reproducible, and testable without database overhead.
63:   * Missing locations return `null` (None) rather than `0.0` so the hybrid matching engine can normalize weights across active signals instead of unfairly penalizing reports without indoor details.
64: * **One thing that could go wrong:**
65:   * If cyclic parent references are permitted in the location tree (e.g. node A made child of node B while B is already a child of A), ancestor traversals and lowest common ancestor searches would loop infinitely, causing server worker starvation; enforcing cycle detection on every `parent_id` mutation neutralizes this hazard.
66: * **Quiz Questions (for viva preparation):**
67:   1. *Why is campus location scoring modeled as a hierarchical tree and adjacency graph rather than pure Euclidean distance between GPS coordinates?*
68:   2. *How does the Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) algorithm determine the similarity score between two locations on campus, and how are adjacent buildings handled?*
69:   3. *Why must missing signals return `null` (None in Python) rather than `0.0` when computing similarity scores in a multimodal retrieval system?*

+## Step 4: Item Reports, Lifecycle Tables, PII Scanner, and Photo Pipeline
+* **Acceptance Criteria:** AC-21 to AC-37
+* **What was built:**
+  * Core lost and found report models (`item_reports`) and photo metadata (`item_images`) with PostgreSQL ENUMs (`report_type`, `report_status`, `time_precision`, `image_role`).
+  * Strict schema validation (`extra="forbid"`) enforcing required title, description, category, and date constraints.
+  * Maximum 3 verification questions/prompts on found items to prevent student friction while verifying rightful owners.
+  * Initial lifecycle state separation: lost reports start in `open`, found reports in `pending_review` until approved.
+  * Pure domain Asia/Kolkata time window computation (`day`, `morning` 06:00-12:00, `afternoon` 12:00-17:00, `evening` 17:00-21:00, `night` 21:00-06:00 crossing midnight, and `exact` +/- 2 hours) returning UTC timestamp ranges.
+  * Exhaustive finite state machine `validate_status_transition` enforcing legitimate state transitions: found (`pending_review` -> `open`/`removed`, `open` -> `in_claim`/`returned`/`archived`/`removed`, `in_claim` -> `open`/`returned`, `returned` = terminal irreversible), lost (`open` -> `matched`/`closed`, `matched` -> `open`/`closed`, `closed` -> `open`).
+  * User closure endpoint allowing reporters to close their own reports; returns HTTP 404 anti-enumeration for non-owners.
+  * Server-side PII Scanner (`backend/app/domain/pii.py`) detecting credit cards via Luhn checksum, 13-19 digit number runs, international & domestic phone numbers, and email addresses in public fields. On detection, rejects with HTTP 422 `pii_detected` without echoing back the sensitive input. Allows PII only in private details fields.
+  * Photo processing pipeline (`backend/app/services/photo.py`): content-type magic bytes verification (ignoring spoofed extensions), 5MB file size limit, 6000x6000 px dimension guard against decompression/pixel bombs, EXIF metadata stripping (including GPS and camera identifiers) using Pillow, image downscaling to <= 1600 px long edge, 256 px thumbnail generation, random UUID storage keys, and 64-bit difference hashing (dHash) for duplicate detection.
+  * Sensitive category protection (`id_card`, `wallet`): photos are automatically marked private and protected from unauthorized public viewing (HTTP 404).
+* **Why it is designed that way:**
+  * Decompression bombs (e.g., a heavily compressed 10000x10000 image taking only 100KB on disk but over 300MB uncompressed in RAM) can quickly exhaust worker memory; inspecting image dimensions before reading full pixel buffers prevents denial-of-service.
+  * EXIF metadata frequently retains exact home/work GPS coordinates and phone camera identifiers; stripping EXIF server-side prevents accidental location disclosure.
+  * When PII is detected in public fields, the API response must NEVER echo the offending number or value back in the error payload, preventing data exfiltration or reflection attacks.
+  * Enforcing explicit `Asia/Kolkata` timezone calculations avoids UTC date truncation bugs where an item lost at 11:00 PM IST is categorized on the wrong UTC calendar day.
+* **One thing that could go wrong:**
+  * If photo files are saved using user-supplied filenames, path traversal attacks (`../../etc/passwd`) or file overwrite vulnerabilities can compromise the host; utilizing UUIDv4 keys and serving images strictly through authenticated streaming endpoints completely decouples user filenames from storage.
+* **Quiz Questions (for viva preparation):**
+  1. *What is a pixel/decompression bomb, and how does the image ingestion pipeline protect server memory before resizing images?*
+  2. *How does the PII scanner detect credit card numbers accurately using the Luhn algorithm, and why must the error response NEVER echo back the detected value?*
+  3. *Why is `returned` modeled as a strictly irreversible terminal state in the found-item lifecycle finite state machine?*

1: # SPEC.md: Smart Campus Lost-and-Found Network
2: 
3: **Version:** 1.0 (draft, based on *Smart Campus Lost-and-Found Network: Project Blueprint*)
4: **Last updated:** 2026-10-18
5: **Methodology:** Spec-Driven Development. Every requirement has an ID, and every acceptance criterion (AC) becomes at least one automated test or one recorded measurement.
6: 
7: > Numbers marked *initial* (thresholds, weights, targets) are starting values. If you change one after measuring, record the change in the Decisions Log (section 20). The results of the evaluation are **findings**, not targets: report whichever way they fall.
8: 
9: ---
10: 
11: ## 1. Overview
12: 
13: A full-stack web application where campus users report lost and found belongings, the system suggests likely matches using text, photos, campus location and time, and campus staff verify claims and complete handovers with a one-time code. AI suggestions are **advice for humans**: no score ever approves a claim or changes a status.
14: 
15: The project has two halves of equal weight. The **product** half is a trustworthy workflow: privacy-aware public listings, evidence-based claims, moderator review, expiring single-use handover codes, an audit trail, and retention rules. The **research** half asks a measurable question: *does combining text, image, location and time signals retrieve lost items better than keyword search?* It is answered on a controlled benchmark with proper splits, confidence intervals and ablations.
16: 
17: The blueprint itself notes that AI-assisted lost-and-found systems already exist. This project does not claim a novel idea. Its contribution is a careful, secure, explainable campus workflow and an honestly measured comparison.
18: 
19: ### Aim
20: 
21: Build a secure, campus-aware lost-and-found platform with explainable multimodal matching, a verified claim and handover process, and a reproducible evaluation of hybrid retrieval against keyword and single-signal baselines, deployed as a service you can open in a browser on your computer or local network.
22: 
23: ### Inputs
24: 
25: | Input | Details |
26: | --- | --- |
27: | Accounts | Campus email, password, display name (optional) |
28: | Reports | Lost or found: title, description, category, time (with precision), campus location (any level), up to 3 photos, optional private details and verification prompts (found reports) |
29: | Claims | Evidence text, answers to verification prompts, up to 3 private evidence photos |
30: | Moderator actions | Approve or remove reports, decide claims, issue and verify handover codes |
31: | Campus data | A location tree and building adjacency, maintained by admins |
32: | Models | A pinned text-embedding model and a pinned image-text model (section 6.1) |
33: | Benchmark data | A synthetic generator plus a small real-photo subset, with a data card (section 7) |
34: | Configuration | Environment variables: database URL, secrets, allowed email domains, SMTP, retention periods, model versions |
35: 
36: ### Outputs
37: 
38: | Output | Details |
39: | --- | --- |
40: | Searchable listings | Found items visible to authenticated campus users, without private details |
41: | Ranked match suggestions | Top candidates for each report, with a score, a bin and a plain-language explanation |
42: | Claims and handovers | Reviewed claims, expiring handover codes, completed returns with an audit trail |
43: | Notifications | In-app and email, with no private details |
44: | Analytics | Recovery rate, time to recovery, unclaimed rate, volume and queue age |
45: | Evaluation results | Tables and plots of retrieval quality, ablations and latency, with confidence intervals and recorded model versions |
46: | Deployed service | The web application, running in containers at `http://localhost:8080` (and over HTTPS on the local network) |
47: 
48: ### Requirements at a glance
49: 
50: - **Functional:** FR-01 to FR-20 (section 14).

306: ## 9. API Contract
307: 
308: **Conventions:** JSON over HTTPS; decimals as strings; timestamps in UTC; `limit` (default 20, maximum 100) and an opaque `cursor`; strict request schemas that forbid unknown fields; a resource that is not yours returns **404**, identical to a missing one. Errors are `{"error": {"code", "message", "details"}}` with 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 410, 413, 415, 422, 423, 429 and 500 used as described in the acceptance criteria.
309: 
310: | Method | Path | Purpose |
311: | --- | --- | --- |
312: | POST | `/api/auth/register`, `/api/auth/login`, `/api/auth/logout`, `/api/auth/verify-email` | Accounts and sessions |
313: | GET, PATCH, DELETE | `/api/me`; GET `/api/me/export` | Profile, notification preferences, export, deletion |
314: | GET, POST | `/api/locations`; PATCH, DELETE `/api/locations/{id}`; POST, DELETE `/api/locations/adjacency` | Location tree (admin writes) |
315: | POST | `/api/reports` | Create a lost or found report |
316: | GET | `/api/reports/mine`, `/api/reports/{id}` | Own reports; a report in the view the caller may see |
317: | PATCH, POST | `/api/reports/{id}`, `/api/reports/{id}/close` | Edit and close |
318: | POST | `/api/reports/{id}/images` | Upload a photo |
319: | GET | `/api/images/{id}` | Authorised image download |
320: | GET | `/api/found` | Public found-item listing, search and filters |
321: | GET | `/api/reports/{id}/matches` | Match suggestions with explanations |
322: | POST | `/api/matches/{id}/dismiss` | "Not mine" |
323: | POST | `/api/found/{id}/claims`; GET `/api/claims/mine`, `/api/claims/{id}`; POST `/api/claims/{id}/withdraw`, `/api/claims/{id}/evidence` | Claims |
324: | GET | `/api/mod/queue` | Pending reports, duplicate flags and claims |
325: | POST | `/api/mod/reports/{id}/approve`, `/api/mod/reports/{id}/remove` | Report moderation |
326: | POST | `/api/mod/claims/{id}/open`, `/approve`, `/reject`, `/request-info` | Claim review |
327: | POST | `/api/mod/handovers/{id}/verify`, `/reissue`, `/complete` | Handover desk |
328: | GET | `/api/notifications`; POST `/api/notifications/{id}/read` | In-app notifications |
329: | GET | `/api/dashboard` | Analytics (moderator and admin) |
330: | GET, PATCH | `/api/admin/users`, `/api/admin/jobs`, `/api/admin/audit`, `/api/admin/evaluation` | Admin |
331: | GET | `/api/health` | Liveness, database and worker status |

105: ## 4. Privacy, Safety and Trust Rules
106: 
107: | ID | Rule |
108: | --- | --- |
109: | **P1 Default-deny public views** | Every response a normal user receives is built from an explicit whitelist of fields. Private details, verification prompts, reporter identity, exact locations, private images, claim evidence, handover codes and hashes never appear in a public view, an explanation, a notification or a log. |
110: | **P2 Private claim evidence** | Evidence and answers are visible only to the claimant and moderators, never to the finder. |
111: | **P3 Data minimisation** | Collect only an email address and an optional display name. No phone number, no student ID, no precise location. |
112: | **P4 Retention** | Found items expire after 90 days unclaimed; photos are deleted 30 days after closure; claim evidence 30 days after the claim closes; audit rows after 365 days (all *initial* and configurable). |
113: | **P5 Anti-scraping** | A login is required to browse, IDs are unguessable, browsing is rate-limited, and new accounts need a verified campus email. |
114: | **P6 Abuse controls** | Per-user claim limits, a flag for repeated rejected claims, and a conflict-of-interest rule for moderators. |
115: | **P7 Evaluation data** | Benchmark data contains no faces or personal data, with consent and licences recorded and a data card. Real users' reports are never used for evaluation. |
116: | **S1 AI is advisory** | Scores and explanations are suggestions. No code path changes a report, claim or handover state because of a score. |
117: | **S2 Human gates** | Found items are published after moderator review (default), claims are decided by a moderator, and handovers are completed by a moderator. |
118: | **S3 Transparent explanations** | Each suggestion shows which signals contributed and how much, in plain language. |
119: | **S4 Sensitive categories** | Items in the categories `id_card` and `wallet` never show photos publicly, and staff handle their details as private. |
120: 
121: ## 5. Domain Rules
122: 
123: ### 5.1 Report lifecycle
124: 
125: **Found report**
126: 
127: | State | Meaning | Legal next states (by whom) |
128: | --- | --- | --- |
129: | `pending_review` | Awaiting moderator approval | `open` (moderator approves), `removed` (moderator) |
130: | `open` | Listed and matchable | `reserved` (system, when a claim is approved), `closed` (reporter or moderator), `removed` (moderator), `unclaimed_expired` (system after the retention period) |
131: | `reserved` | A claim is approved and a handover is pending | `returned` (system, on handover completion), `open` (system, if the handover is cancelled or expires) |
132: | `returned` | Handed over | none |
133: | `unclaimed_expired` | Not claimed in time; a disposition is recorded | none |
134: | `closed`, `removed` | Ended by the reporter or a moderator | none |
135: 
136: **Lost report**
137: 
138: | State | Legal next states (by whom) |
139: | --- | --- |
140: | `open` | `resolved` (system on a completed handover, or the reporter), `closed` (reporter), `removed` (moderator), `expired` (system) |
141: | `resolved`, `closed`, `removed`, `expired` | none |
142: 
143: Every other transition returns 409 `invalid_transition`. A `reserved` item is excluded from matching and from new claims (409 `item_reserved`).

58: class LoginRateLimiter:
59:     """In-memory rate limiter for failed login attempts (SEC6, AC-04)."""
60: 
61:     def __init__(self, max_attempts: int = 5, window_seconds: int = 900) -> None:
62:         self.max_attempts = max_attempts
63:         self.window_seconds = window_seconds
64:         # key: identifier -> list of failure timestamps
65:         self.attempts: dict[str, list[float]] = {}
66: 
67:     def _clean_old_attempts(self, key: str, now: float) -> list[float]:
68:         if key not in self.attempts:
69:             return []
70:         valid = [t for t in self.attempts[key] if now - t < self.window_seconds]
71:         if valid:
72:             self.attempts[key] = valid
73:         else:
74:             self.attempts.pop(key, None)
75:         return valid
76: 
77:     def is_rate_limited(self, key: str) -> tuple[bool, int]:
78:         """Check if key is rate limited. Returns (is_limited, retry_after_seconds)."""
79:         now = time.time()
80:         valid = self._clean_old_attempts(key, now)
81:         if len(valid) >= self.max_attempts:
82:             oldest = valid[0]
83:             retry_after = max(1, int(self.window_seconds - (now - oldest)))
84:             return True, retry_after
85:         return False, 0
86: 
87:     def record_failure(self, key: str) -> None:
88:         now = time.time()
89:         valid = self._clean_old_attempts(key, now)
90:         valid.append(now)
91:         self.attempts[key] = valid
92: 
93:     def reset(self, key: str) -> None:
94:         self.attempts.pop(key, None)

11:     name: str
12:     kind: LocationKind
13:     parent: "LocationNode | None" = None
14: 
15: 
16: def _get_ancestor_chain(node: LocationNode) -> list[LocationNode]:
17:     """Return the chain of nodes from the current node up to the root."""
18:     chain: list[LocationNode] = []
19:     curr: LocationNode | None = node
20:     while curr is not None:
21:         chain.append(curr)
22:         curr = curr.parent
23:     return chain
24: 
25: 
26: def calculate_location_score(
27:     loc_a: LocationNode | None,
28:     loc_b: LocationNode | None,
29:     adjacency_set: set[tuple[uuid.UUID, uuid.UUID]] | None = None,
30: ) -> float | None:
31:     """[LEARN] Pure domain location scoring function per Spec 6.3 and AC-18.
32: 
33:     Scores the relationship between two locations in a campus tree:
34:     - 1.0: Identical location
35:     - 0.8: One is an ancestor of the other
36:     - 0.7: Share a floor or an area (LCA is floor or area)
37:     - 0.6: Share a building only (LCA is building)
38:     - 0.5: Different buildings that are adjacent
39:     - 0.2: Same campus, not adjacent
40:     - 0.0: Different campuses
41:     - None (null): Either location is missing
42:     """
43:     if loc_a is None or loc_b is None:
44:         return None
45: 
46:     # 1. Identical location
47:     if loc_a.id == loc_b.id:
48:         return 1.0
49: 
50:     chain_a = _get_ancestor_chain(loc_a)
51:     chain_b = _get_ancestor_chain(loc_b)
52: 
53:     # 2. One is an ancestor of the other
54:     ancestor_ids_a = {node.id for node in chain_a[1:]}
55:     ancestor_ids_b = {node.id for node in chain_b[1:]}
56: 
57:     if loc_a.id in ancestor_ids_b or loc_b.id in ancestor_ids_a:
58:         return 0.8
59: 
60:     # 3. Find Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA)
61:     ids_b = {node.id for node in chain_b}
62:     lca: LocationNode | None = None
63:     for node in chain_a:
64:         if node.id in ids_b:
65:             lca = node
66:             break
67: 
68:     # If roots differ (no common ancestor or different campus roots)
69:     if lca is None:
70:         return 0.0
71: 
72:     # Share a floor or an area (LCA is floor or area)
73:     if lca.kind in ("floor", "area", "room"):
74:         return 0.7
75: 
76:     # Share a building only (LCA is building)
77:     if lca.kind == "building":
78:         return 0.6
79: 
80:     # LCA is campus: check building adjacency
81:     if lca.kind == "campus":
82:         # Find building ancestor for loc_a and loc_b
83:         bldg_a = next((node for node in chain_a if node.kind == "building"), None)
84:         bldg_b = next((node for node in chain_b if node.kind == "building"), None)
85: 
86:         if bldg_a is not None and bldg_b is not None and bldg_a.id != bldg_b.id:
87:             adj = adjacency_set or set()
88:             is_adjacent = (bldg_a.id, bldg_b.id) in adj or (bldg_b.id, bldg_a.id) in adj
89:             if is_adjacent:
90:                 return 0.5
91: 
92:         return 0.2
93: 
94:     return 0.0

+## Step 5: Browsing, Search, and Whitelisted Public Views
+* **Acceptance Criteria:** AC-38 to AC-44
+* **What was built:**
+  * Whitelisted public found-item listing (`GET /api/found`) showing strictly `open` found items (excluding `pending_review`, `removed`, `returned`, `archived`, `closed`, and all lost reports) with building-level locations, public descriptions, category, dates, and public photo thumbnails.
+  * Strict Default-Deny Serializers (`PublicFoundItemSummary` and `PublicReportDetailResponse`) with `extra="forbid"`, verified by automated canary contract testing ensuring zero leakage of private details, verification prompts, reporter identities (ID/email/name), finer-than-building locations (room/floor), or private images.
+  * Role-based report detail routing (`GET /api/reports/{id}`): returns full staff report view (`FullStaffReportResponse`) to moderators, admins, and the report's owner; returns whitelisted public detail view to non-owner student users for open found reports; and returns HTTP 404 anti-enumeration on lost reports or non-open found reports accessed by other users.
+  * PostgreSQL full-text search across `title` and `description` via `to_tsvector` and `plainto_tsquery`, backed by an indexed GIN expression (`0005_search_index.py`).
+  * Hierarchical building filter resolving all descendant locations (floors, rooms, areas) via recursive Common Table Expression (CTE).
+  * Multi-attribute filtering combining full-text search, category, building descendants, and date ranges with `AND`.
+  * Stable cursor pagination encoding `(created_at, id)` as an opaque base64 string with configurable limit (default 20, max 100) guaranteeing no skipped or duplicated items across pages during real-time writes.
+  * Per-user browse rate limiting via `BrowseRateLimiter` allowing 120 requests/minute and returning HTTP 429 with standard `Retry-After` header when exceeded.
+  * Strict campus authentication (401 for anonymous) and UUIDv4 identifier enforcement across all browse endpoints.
+* **Why it is designed that way:**
+  * A default-deny serializer ensures that even if developers add new internal or sensitive columns to the database model in future steps, those columns will never accidentally leak to public API callers unless explicitly whitelisted in the response schema.
+  * Resolving locations to building-level for public viewers protects student safety by preventing stalkers or opportunistic claimants from learning the exact room or floor where an item was lost or found.
+  * Stable cursor pagination based on `(created_at, id)` avoids the offset pagination trap (e.g., `OFFSET 20`), where items inserted while a user is browsing cause page drift and duplicate or missing items.
+  * Opaque cursor strings prevent clients from relying on internal database sorting implementations, allowing future backend optimizations without breaking client contracts.
+* **One thing that could go wrong:**
+  * If a user passes dates with ambiguous timezone offsets or plain calendar dates `YYYY-MM-DD`, naive parsing can truncate queries at midnight `00:00:00`, excluding all items found during the daytime on the end date; explicitly expanding `date_to` to `23:59:59.999999 UTC` guarantees inclusive date window filtering.
+* **Quiz Questions (for viva preparation):**
+  1. *What is a "default-deny serializer", and how does contract testing with canary strings guarantee that sensitive student data cannot leak into public API responses?*
+  2. *Why is cursor-based pagination using a composite tuple `(created_at, id)` preferred over traditional `OFFSET`/`LIMIT` pagination in high-frequency lost-and-found databases?*
+  3. *How does the building filter use a recursive Common Table Expression (CTE) to include items located on lower hierarchical levels (such as specific rooms or floors) without exposing those finer locations to the public?*

### Step 5 Completed: Browsing, Search, and Whitelisted Public Views (AC-38 to AC-44)

We have implemented and verified all acceptance criteria for **Step 5** using strict Test-Driven Development (TDD).

---

### What Was Built & Verified

1. **Whitelisted Found-Item Listing (`GET /api/found`) (AC-38):**
   - Strictly shows `open` found items; excludes `pending_review`, `removed`, `returned`, `archived`, `closed`, and all lost reports.
   - Outputs building-level locations, public descriptions, category, date, and public image thumbnails.
2. **Default-Deny Contract Testing (AC-39):**
   - Implemented `PublicFoundItemSummary` and `PublicReportDetailResponse` with Pydantic `extra="forbid"`.
   - Automated canary contract tests verify that `private_details`, `verification_prompts`, `reporter_id`/email/name, finer-than-building locations (rooms/floors), and private images are never leaked.
3. **Lost Reports Privacy & Anti-Enumeration (AC-40):**
   - Lost reports are visible strictly to their reporter, moderators, and admins.
   - Access attempts by other students return HTTP 404 (anti-enumeration).
4. **Full-Text Search & Multi-Filter Query Engine (AC-41):**
   - PostgreSQL full-text search across `title` and `description` via `to_tsvector` and `plainto_tsquery`, backed by a dedicated GIN expression index ([0005_search_index.py](file:///c:/Users/abhir/OneDrive/Desktop/AIDS/Campus%20lost%20and%20found/backend/alembic/versions/0005_search_index.py)).
   - Recursive Common Table Expression (CTE) in [backend/app/services/location.py](file:///c:/Users/abhir/OneDrive/Desktop/AIDS/Campus%20lost%20and%20found/backend/app/services/location.py) resolves all descendant locations (floors, rooms, areas) for building filters.
   - Combined filters (`q`, `category`, `building_id`, `date_from`, `date_to`) evaluate with `AND`.
   - Stable cursor pagination encoding `(created_at, id)` as an opaque base64 cursor.
5. **Staff Full Details Access (AC-42):**
   - Moderators, admins, and the report's owner receive [FullStaffReportResponse](file:///c:/Users/abhir/OneDrive/Desktop/AIDS/Campus%20lost%20and%20found/backend/app/schemas/found.py) with `private_details`, `verification_prompts`, exact room/floor location, reporter info, and all photos.
6. **Browse Rate Limiting & Auth Guarantees (AC-43, AC-44):**
   - In-memory sliding window rate limiter ([backend/app/core/rate_limit.py](file:///c:/Users/abhir/OneDrive/Desktop/AIDS/Campus%20lost%20and%20found/backend/app/core/rate_limit.py)) enforcing 120 requests/minute per user with `HTTP 429 Too Many Requests` and standard `Retry-After` header.
   - Campus authentication required (HTTP 401 for anonymous) and UUIDv4 validation across all endpoints.

184: ## 6. Matching
185: 
186: ### 6.1 Models and embeddings
187: 
188: | Purpose | Starting choice (verify each licence before use) |
189: | --- | --- |
190: | Text embeddings | A small sentence-embedding model such as `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (384 dimensions) |
191: | Image and cross-modal embeddings | A CLIP-family model such as ViT-B/32 (512 dimensions), giving image vectors and text vectors in one space |
192: | Stretch comparison | A SigLIP-family model, as the blueprint suggests |
193: 
194: - Weights are downloaded **at image build time** with pinned revisions and checksums and baked into the image, so the running system makes no outbound model calls (D4).
195: - Every embedding row stores `model_name`, `model_version` and `dimension`, and vectors are L2-normalised. Matching compares only vectors of the same version. Vectors live in PostgreSQL with the **pgvector** extension and an HNSW index using cosine distance.
196: - Embeddings are computed by background workers, never during a web request.
197: 
198: ### 6.2 Signals
199: 
200: Each signal is a number in [0, 1] or `null` when it cannot be computed.
201: 
202: | Signal | Definition |
203: | --- | --- |
204: | Text | `max(0, cosine)` between the text embeddings of `category + title + description` |
205: | Image | Image-to-image `max(0, cosine)` when both reports have photos (the best pair of photos); otherwise text-to-image `max(0, cosine)` (a report's text against the other report's photo) when exactly one has photos; otherwise `null` |
206: | Location | The table in 6.3 |
207: | Time | The decay function in 6.3 |

100: ## Step 5: Browsing, Search, and Whitelisted Public Views
101: * **Acceptance Criteria:** AC-38 to AC-44
102: * **What was built:**
103:   * Whitelisted public found-item listing (`GET /api/found`) showing strictly `open` found items (excluding `pending_review`, `removed`, `returned`, `archived`, `closed`, and all lost reports) with building-level locations, public descriptions, category, dates, and public photo thumbnails.
104:   * Strict Default-Deny Serializers (`PublicFoundItemSummary` and `PublicReportDetailResponse`) with `extra="forbid"`, verified by automated canary contract testing ensuring zero leakage of private details, verification prompts, reporter identities (ID/email/name), finer-than-building locations (room/floor), or private images.
105:   * Role-based report detail routing (`GET /api/reports/{id}`): returns full staff report view (`FullStaffReportResponse`) to moderators, admins, and the report's owner; returns whitelisted public detail view to non-owner student users for open found reports; and returns HTTP 404 anti-enumeration on lost reports or non-open found reports accessed by other users.
106:   * PostgreSQL full-text search across `title` and `description` via `to_tsvector` and `plainto_tsquery`, backed by an indexed GIN expression (`0005_search_index.py`).
107:   * Hierarchical building filter resolving all descendant locations (floors, rooms, areas) via recursive Common Table Expression (CTE).
108:   * Multi-attribute filtering combining full-text search, category, building descendants, and date ranges with `AND`.
109:   * Stable cursor pagination encoding `(created_at, id)` as an opaque base64 string with configurable limit (default 20, max 100) guaranteeing no skipped or duplicated items across pages during real-time writes.
110:   * Per-user browse rate limiting via `BrowseRateLimiter` allowing 120 requests/minute and returning HTTP 429 with standard `Retry-After` header when exceeded.
111:   * Strict campus authentication (401 for anonymous) and UUIDv4 identifier enforcement across all browse endpoints.
112: * **Why it is designed that way:**
113:   * A default-deny serializer ensures that even if developers add new internal or sensitive columns to the database model in future steps, those columns will never accidentally leak to public API callers unless explicitly whitelisted in the response schema.
114:   * Resolving locations to building-level for public viewers protects student safety by preventing stalkers or opportunistic claimants from learning the exact room or floor where an item was lost or found.
115:   * Stable cursor pagination based on `(created_at, id)` avoids the offset pagination trap (e.g., `OFFSET 20`), where items inserted while a user is browsing cause page drift and duplicate or missing items.
116:   * Opaque cursor strings prevent clients from relying on internal database sorting implementations, allowing future backend optimizations without breaking client contracts.
117: * **One thing that could go wrong:**
118:   * If a user passes dates with ambiguous timezone offsets or plain calendar dates `YYYY-MM-DD`, naive parsing can truncate queries at midnight `00:00:00`, excluding all items found during the daytime on the end date; explicitly expanding `date_to` to `23:59:59.999999 UTC` guarantees inclusive date window filtering.
119: * **Quiz Questions (for viva preparation):**
120:   1. *What is a "default-deny serializer", and how does contract testing with canary strings guarantee that sensitive student data cannot leak into public API responses?*
121:   2. *Why is cursor-based pagination using a composite tuple `(created_at, id)` preferred over traditional `OFFSET`/`LIMIT` pagination in high-frequency lost-and-found databases?*
122:   3. *How does the building filter use a recursive Common Table Expression (CTE) to include items located on lower hierarchical levels (such as specific rooms or floors) without exposing those finer locations to the public?*

+## Step 6: Background Jobs, Model Registry, and Notification Outbox
+* **Acceptance Criteria:** AC-45 to AC-50, AC-68 to AC-74
+* **What was built:**
+  * **Database Infrastructure & Migration (`0006_jobs_embed_notifs.py`):**
+    * Background job queue table (`jobs`) with composite index `(status, run_after)` supporting worker polling and exponential retry backoff.
+    * Model registry (`model_registry`) and pgvector tables (`report_text_embeddings` with `vector(384)`, `report_image_embeddings` with `vector(512)`) enforcing unique version constraints `(entity_id, model_name, model_version)`.
+    * Transactional notification outbox table (`notifications`) with unique constraint `uq_notifications_event_key` and per-user index.
+  * **Transactional Background Job Enqueueing (AC-45):**
+    * Saving a lost or found report transactional-enqueues `embed_report_text`, and uploading a photo transactional-enqueues `embed_report_image`.
+    * Fast return latency (< 300 ms with models off or mock embeddings).
+  * **Concurrent Lock-Free Queue Workers (AC-46):**
+    * `claim_jobs()` worker engine using PostgreSQL `SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` ensuring multiple concurrent workers never process or duplicate the same job (verified with 2 concurrent workers claiming 200 jobs with zero overlap).
+  * **Retry Backoff & Admin Controls (AC-47):**
+    * Structured exponential backoff retry policy (`[1, 2, 4, 8]` minutes, max 5 attempts); transitions to `failed` upon the 5th failure.
+    * Admin job inspection (`GET /api/admin/jobs`) and manual retry (`POST /api/admin/jobs/{id}/retry`) resetting attempts and status for failed jobs.
+  * **Embedding Model Registry & Backfill (AC-48, AC-49, AC-50):**
+    * Idempotent vector insertion (`upsert_report_text_embedding` / `upsert_report_image_embedding`).
+    * Model activation workflow (`activate_model_version` and `POST /api/admin/models/activate`) that sets the active version and enqueues backfill jobs across all open reports.
+    * Database-level pgvector dimension validation (verifying PostgreSQL strictly rejects mismatched vector dimensions).
+  * **Transactional Notification Outbox & Deduplication (AC-68, AC-69, AC-70):**
+    * Transactional consistency: rolling back a business transaction automatically aborts notification creation, preventing ghost emails.
+    * Idempotent deduplication on `event_key` guaranteeing duplicate events produce a single notification record.
+    * Deterministic RFC 5322 `Message-ID` generation (`<event_key@campus.domain>`) enabling client-side email threading and duplicate suppression.
+    * SMTP delivery error handling with retry backoff and failure state logging.
+  * **Notification Privacy & User Preferences (AC-71, AC-72, AC-73):**
+    * Whitelisted notification template rendering with automated canary verification: private details, verification prompts, and student PII are never leaked in email subjects or bodies.
+    * Preference enforcement: user opt-out (`notify_matches: false`) skips match emails while preserving critical claim/handover communications.
+    * Spam protection: hard cap of 5 match suggestion emails per user per 24-hour window.
+  * **In-App Notification API (AC-74):**
+    * Paginated, owner-only notification inbox (`GET /api/notifications`) with filters (`status=all|unread|read`) and stable cursor pagination.
+    * Read receipt tracking (`POST /api/notifications/{id}/read`) with 404 anti-enumeration against other users' notifications.
+* **Why it is designed that way:**
+  * **Transactional Outbox Pattern:** By writing job records and notifications into PostgreSQL within the same database transaction as reports and claims, we solve the dual-write problem. If the transaction aborts, no orphaned jobs or emails are sent. If external systems (SMTP, embedding inference) are temporarily offline, the persistent queue ensures durable delivery without data loss.
+  * **`SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`:** PostgreSQL natively coordinates concurrent workers without distributed locking (Redis, ZooKeeper). Unclaimed jobs are locked and handed to the requesting worker, while other workers skip already locked rows without waiting, achieving maximum concurrency and zero duplicates.
+  * **Model Registry Decoupling:** Storing model names, versions, and embedding dimensions in a model registry decouples ML model lifecycle from application code. Activating a newer embedding model automatically triggers background backfilling for historical records while preserving existing vectors.
+  * **Canonical Event Keys:** Using deterministic event keys (e.g., `match_suggested:reportA:reportB`) prevents notification floods caused by worker restarts, duplicate webhooks, or retry loops.
+* **One thing that could go wrong:**
+  * **Alembic Revision ID Column Width:** PostgreSQL `alembic_version.version_num` is a `VARCHAR(32)` column. Migration revision IDs exceeding 32 characters (e.g. `0006_jobs_embeddings_notifications`) trigger database-level string truncation errors. Keeping revision identifiers concise (e.g., `0006_jobs_embed_notifs`) prevents deployment failures.
+  * **ORM ID Population Timing:** In SQLAlchemy, auto-generated UUIDs on models are populated only upon database insert or flush. Accessing `model.id` before flush produces `None`. Explicitly passing `id=uuid.uuid4()` at instantiation ensures `entity_id` is never null when enqueuing background jobs.
+* **Quiz Questions (for viva preparation):**
+  1. *How does PostgreSQL's `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` provide a reliable, concurrent work queue without requiring an external message broker like Redis or RabbitMQ?*
+  2. *What is the Transactional Outbox Pattern, and how does it prevent the "dual-write" consistency hazard between relational databases and external services like email or ML workers?*
+  3. *Why should background job retry intervals use exponential backoff (e.g., 1, 2, 4, 8 minutes) instead of immediate or fixed-interval retries?*

8: Follow the build order in section 19 of the spec, one step at a time. Finish a step (all its acceptance criteria passing) before starting the next. Do not stop in the middle of a step unless you are blocked, a [LEARN] module comes up, or the spec has an open question you need me to answer.
9: Tests first. For each acceptance criterion, write the failing test, then the code that makes it pass. Name each test after its AC ID (for example test_ac_53_hybrid_example).
10: Derive expected values by calculation, as the acceptance criteria do. Never copy the application's own output into a test as the expected answer, and never edit a test value or a threshold to make a test pass. If a test seems wrong, tell me.
11: Fast tests use fixed stand-in embeddings, so the normal suite needs no model downloads. Tests that use the real models are marked slow.
12: Run all checks after every change: formatting, lint, type checks, migrations and tests. Show me the results at the end of each step.
13: Move fast. Do not pause for review between modules. At the end of each step, give me a short summary: files changed, tests passing, anything I should check.
14: Ask before deciding. If the spec leaves a choice open (section 21), ask me. When we decide, add a row to the Decisions Log in SPEC.md and to DECISIONS.md.
15: Do not add features that are not in the spec. Suggest them at the end instead.
16: Learning rules
17: At the end of each step, add a short entry to docs/learning-log.md: what was built, why it is designed that way, one thing that could go wrong, and 3 quiz questions for me (no answers; I will answer them myself).
18: These modules are marked [LEARN]. For them, first explain the design and the key edge cases in a few sentences, then let me write the first version myself and review it afterwards:
19: The location and time scores, and the hybrid score with missing signals and its explanations (spec sections 6.3 to 6.6)
20: The handover code: generation, HMAC storage, normalisation, attempts and expiry (spec section 5.4)
21: The evaluation metrics, bootstrap and paired bootstrap (spec sections 7.3 and 7.4)
22: The whitelist serialisers and the role and ownership checks (spec sections 3, 4 and 12)
23: If I say "you write it" for a [LEARN] module, write it, and still add its learning-log entry.
24: If I ask "why", explain with a small concrete example, not just a definition.
25: Safety, privacy and integrity rules (never relax these)
26: AI is advisory. Never write code that changes a report, claim or handover state because of a score.
27: Default-deny serialisers. Every response a normal user sees is built from an explicit whitelist. Private details, verification prompts, reporter identity, exact locations, private images, claim evidence, handover codes and hashes must never appear in a public view, an explanation, a notification or a log. Use canary strings in tests.
28: Handover codes: secure random generation, store only the HMAC, constant-time comparison, never log or return a code except to the approved claimant.
29: No real student data. Use only synthetic data and the consented evaluation subsets. Never invent photos, consent records or licences, and ask me for any dataset or model whose licence you cannot confirm.
30: Evaluation integrity. Never tune on the test set or give tuning code a path to it. Never edit results or choose a configuration after seeing test results. Record the hypotheses first and report the outcome whichever way it falls. Never fabricate or round up benchmark numbers.
31: Models: pin versions and checksums, bake them into the images, and make the running backend and worker work with no outbound network access.
32: Project rules
33: Layering: the domain package contains pure functions with no framework, database, model or clock imports. Routers are thin; rules live in services and the domain package.
34: Identity and roles: derive them from the session only. Request schemas forbid unknown fields. Foreign resources return 404.
35: Consistency: write state changes together with their notifications and jobs in one transaction (outbox). Workers claim jobs with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and must be idempotent.
36: Time: store UTC, inject the clock, and compute local days in the user's IANA timezone.
37: Secrets: only in environment variables. Never commit .env. Never log passwords, tokens, codes or full emails.
38: Uploads: decide the file type by content, guard pixel counts, strip metadata, re-encode, store under random keys, and serve only through the authorised route.
39: Dependencies: pin versions, and ask before adding a new dependency.
40: Tests use PostgreSQL with pgvector, never SQLite.
41: Deployment: the project must always run with Docker Compose (spec section 13). Build the walking-skeleton stack in step 1, keep it working, and rebuild after each step. Application containers run as non-root, and credentials from non-localhost clients are accepted only over TLS.

1: # SPEC.md: Smart Campus Lost-and-Found Network
2: 
3: **Version:** 1.0 (draft, based on *Smart Campus Lost-and-Found Network: Project Blueprint*)
4: **Last updated:** 2026-10-18
5: **Methodology:** Spec-Driven Development. Every requirement has an ID, and every acceptance criterion (AC) becomes at least one automated test or one recorded measurement.
6: 
7: > Numbers marked *initial* (thresholds, weights, targets) are starting values. If you change one after measuring, record the change in the Decisions Log (section 20). The results of the evaluation are **findings**, not targets: report whichever way they fall.
8: 
9: ---
10: 
11: ## 1. Overview
12: 
13: A full-stack web application where campus users report lost and found belongings, the system suggests likely matches using text, photos, campus location and time, and campus staff verify claims and complete handovers with a one-time code. AI suggestions are **advice for humans**: no score ever approves a claim or changes a status.
14: 
15: The project has two halves of equal weight. The **product** half is a trustworthy workflow: privacy-aware public listings, evidence-based claims, moderator review, expiring single-use handover codes, an audit trail, and retention rules. The **research** half asks a measurable question: *does combining text, image, location and time signals retrieve lost items better than keyword search?* It is answered on a controlled benchmark with proper splits, confidence intervals and ablations.
16: 
17: The blueprint itself notes that AI-assisted lost-and-found systems already exist. This project does not claim a novel idea. Its contribution is a careful, secure, explainable campus workflow and an honestly measured comparison.
18: 
19: ### Aim
20: 
21: Build a secure, campus-aware lost-and-found platform with explainable multimodal matching, a verified claim and handover process, and a reproducible evaluation of hybrid retrieval against keyword and single-signal baselines, deployed as a service you can open in a browser on your computer or local network.
22: 
23: ### Inputs
24: 
25: | Input | Details |
26: | --- | --- |
27: | Accounts | Campus email, password, display name (optional) |
28: | Reports | Lost or found: title, description, category, time (with precision), campus location (any level), up to 3 photos, optional private details and verification prompts (found reports) |
29: | Claims | Evidence text, answers to verification prompts, up to 3 private evidence photos |
30: | Moderator actions | Approve or remove reports, decide claims, issue and verify handover codes |
31: | Campus data | A location tree and building adjacency, maintained by admins |
32: | Models | A pinned text-embedding model and a pinned image-text model (section 6.1) |
33: | Benchmark data | A synthetic generator plus a small real-photo subset, with a data card (section 7) |
34: | Configuration | Environment variables: database URL, secrets, allowed email domains, SMTP, retention periods, model versions |
35: 
36: ### Outputs
37: 
38: | Output | Details |
39: | --- | --- |
40: | Searchable listings | Found items visible to authenticated campus users, without private details |
41: | Ranked match suggestions | Top candidates for each report, with a score, a bin and a plain-language explanation |
42: | Claims and handovers | Reviewed claims, expiring handover codes, completed returns with an audit trail |
43: | Notifications | In-app and email, with no private details |
44: | Analytics | Recovery rate, time to recovery, unclaimed rate, volume and queue age |
45: | Evaluation results | Tables and plots of retrieval quality, ablations and latency, with confidence intervals and recorded model versions |
46: | Deployed service | The web application, running in containers at `http://localhost:8080` (and over HTTPS on the local network) |

56: ## 2. Goals, Scope and Non-Goals
57: 
58: **Goals**
59: 1. Accounts with roles (user, moderator, admin) and campus-email verification.
60: 2. A hierarchical campus location model that tolerates approximate locations.
61: 3. Lost and found reports with a safe photo pipeline and a defined lifecycle.
62: 4. Searchable listings that never expose private details.
63: 5. Background embedding jobs and a hybrid matching engine with explanations.
64: 6. Notifications (in-app and email) through a reliable outbox.
65: 7. Claims, moderator review, and one-time handover codes.
66: 8. An append-only audit log, retention rules, and data export and deletion.
67: 9. An analytics dashboard.
68: 10. A reproducible evaluation of keyword, text, image and hybrid retrieval.
69: 11. A tested, documented, deployed system.
70: 
71: **Non-goals (v1)**
72: - Campus single sign-on, mobile apps, push notifications, or SMS.
73: - Automatic ownership decisions, or any AI action without human review.
74: - GPS tracking or precise indoor positioning.
75: - Facial recognition. Photos are never used to identify people.
76: - Evidence that the system improves real-world recovery rates (only a pilot could show that; the benchmark does not).
77: 
78: **Stretch** (only after every required criterion passes): a SigLIP-family model comparison, multilingual text, face and number-plate blurring in photos, learning from dismissals, campus SSO, and a digest email.
79: 
80: ## 3. Roles and Access Control
81: 
82: | Role | Who | Can |
83: | --- | --- | --- |
84: | `user` | A verified campus account | Report items, browse found items, see matches for their own lost reports, claim found items, manage their own data |
85: | `moderator` | Authorised campus staff | Everything a user can, plus review reports and images, decide claims, issue and verify handover codes, see private details and the dashboard |
86: | `admin` | A small number of administrators | Everything a moderator can, plus manage locations, roles, jobs, the audit log and the evaluation page |
87: 
88: | Capability | Anonymous | User | Moderator | Admin |
89: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
90: | Register, verify email, log in | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
91: | Browse found items (public view) | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
92: | Create lost or found reports | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
93: | See own reports and matches | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
94: | See other users' lost reports | No | No | Yes | Yes |
95: | See private details and exact location of a found report | No | Reporter only | Yes | Yes |
96: | Approve or remove reports and images | No | No | Yes | Yes |
97: | Submit a claim (not on their own found item) | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
98: | See claim evidence | No | Claimant only | Yes | Yes |
99: | Decide claims (subject to the conflict rule) | No | No | Yes | Yes |
100: | Issue, reissue and verify handover codes | No | No | Yes | Yes |

672: ## 18. Testing Strategy
673: 
674: | Layer | What it checks |

715: ## 20. Decisions Log
716: 
717: | ID | Date | Decision | Alternatives | Why |
718: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
719: | D-01 | 2026-10-18 | AI is advisory: scores never change a state | Auto-approve high scores | Ownership needs human judgement, and false claims are the main risk |
720: | D-02 | 2026-10-18 | Lost reports are private; only found reports are browsable | Public lost reports | Lost reports reveal owners and valuables, and browsing found items helps owners |
721: | D-03 | 2026-10-18 | Found reports and photos are moderated before publication (configurable) | Publish immediately | Stops spam, personal data in photos, and stolen-property listings |
722: | D-04 | 2026-10-18 | Missing signals are excluded and weights renormalised | Treat missing as zero | A missing photo is not evidence of a mismatch |
723: | D-05 | 2026-10-18 | The time score is asymmetric (steeper when found before lost) | Symmetric decay | Reflects that a thing cannot be found before it is lost, apart from imprecise reporting |
724: | D-06 | 2026-10-18 | A location-tree score with an adjacency table | GPS distance | Works indoors, tolerates approximate reports, and needs no precise location data |
725: | D-07 | 2026-10-18 | Embeddings are computed by workers, and models are baked into the images | Compute in requests; download models at runtime | Fast requests, offline operation, and pinned reproducible models |
726: | D-08 | 2026-10-18 | pgvector with HNSW in PostgreSQL | A separate vector database | One database to run, back up and secure; recall against exact search is measured |
727: | D-09 | 2026-10-18 | 8-character codes (40 bits), HMAC-stored, 5 attempts, 48-hour expiry | 6-digit numeric codes | A far smaller guessing chance (about 4.5 × 10⁻¹²) for the same effort at the desk |
728: | D-10 | 2026-10-18 | Server-side sessions with CSRF tokens | Stateless JWTs | Revocable, and not readable by scripts |
729: | D-11 | 2026-10-18 | A synthetic benchmark plus small real-photo and human-written subsets | Real users' reports | Privacy, consent and reproducibility; the limits are stated |
730: | D-12 | 2026-10-18 | Development-only tuning with a frozen configuration | Tune on all data | Prevents leakage, and the test run stays honest |
731: | D-13 | 2026-10-18 | Bootstrap confidence intervals and paired differences | Single-number comparison | Shows whether a difference is real |
732: | D-14 | 2026-10-18 | An append-only audit table enforced in the database | Application-level logging | Moderation and handover events must be trustworthy |
733: | D-15 | 2026-10-18 | A job queue and notification outbox in PostgreSQL | A message broker | No extra service, with transactional consistency |
734: | D-16 | 2026-10-18 | Credentials only over TLS beyond localhost, with a private certificate authority | Plain HTTP on the network | Passwords and sessions must not be readable on the network |

200: Each signal is a number in [0, 1] or `null` when it cannot be computed.
201: 
202: | Signal | Definition |
203: | --- | --- |
204: | Text | `max(0, cosine)` between the text embeddings of `category + title + description` |
205: | Image | Image-to-image `max(0, cosine)` when both reports have photos (the best pair of photos); otherwise text-to-image `max(0, cosine)` (a report's text against the other report's photo) when exactly one has photos; otherwise `null` |
206: | Location | The table in 6.3 |
207: | Time | The decay function in 6.3 |
208: 
209: ### 6.3 Location and time scores
210: 
211: **Location score** by the relationship between the two locations in the tree:
212: 
213: | Relationship | Score |
214: | --- | --- |
215: | Identical | 1.0 |
216: | One is an ancestor of the other | 0.8 |
217: | Share a floor or an area (lowest common ancestor is a floor or an area) | 0.7 |
218: | Share a building only | 0.6 |
219: | Different buildings that are adjacent | 0.5 |
220: | Same campus, not adjacent | 0.2 |
221: | Different campuses | 0.0 |
222: | A location is missing | `null` |
223: 
224: **Time score** compares the two windows. If they overlap, the score is 1. Otherwise let `gap` be the hours between them: if the found window is after the lost window, `score = exp(−gap / 48)`; if it is before, `score = exp(−gap / 6)`. The asymmetry reflects that a finder cannot find something before it was lost, apart from imprecise reporting.
225: 
226: ### 6.4 Hybrid score
227: 
228: `score = Σ wᵢ sᵢ / Σ wᵢ`, summed **only over signals that are not `null`**. Initial weights: text 0.40, image 0.35, location 0.15, time 0.10. Missing signals are excluded, never treated as zero. Each stored candidate records its weights version. Bins: at least 0.75 `high`, at least 0.55 `medium`, otherwise `low`. A match notification is sent only for a score of at least 0.65 ranked in the top 3. Weights and thresholds are tuned on the development set only (section 7).
229: 
230: ### 6.5 Candidates and retrieval
231: 
232: A candidate pair is a lost report and a found report where both are `open`, the reporters differ, the pair has not been dismissed, and the found time lies between 6 hours before the lost window starts and 30 days after it ends. Retrieval uses the HNSW index to fetch the nearest neighbours by text and by image, merges them with the location and time candidates, scores them all, and returns the top K (default 10). New reports trigger scoring in both directions, and each (lost, found, model version, weights version) is scored once. Ties break by the older found report, then by ID.
233: 
234: ### 6.6 Explanations
235: 
236: The contribution of a signal is `wᵢ sᵢ / Σ wⱼ` over the available signals, so contributions sum to the score. The explanation lists the signals contributing at least 10% of the score (or the top 3) in plain sentences, for example "Similar description", "Visually similar photo", "Reported in a nearby building", and "Found 3 hours after you reported it lost". It never includes private details.
237: 
238: ## 7. Evaluation Design
239: 
240: **Research question:** does combining image similarity, semantic text similarity, and campus location and time signals improve lost-item retrieval compared with keyword-based search?
241: 
242: ### 7.1 Benchmark
243: 
244: - **Items:** 300 true items across the 12 categories, each with a lost report and a found report, plus 100 **background** found reports with no lost report (unclaimed items). A fixed campus tree of about 40 leaf locations is used.
245: - **Synthetic text:** each side is generated by a seeded grammar from the item's attributes (category, colour, material or brand-like descriptor, distinguishing feature). The lost and found sides use **different** lexicons and phrasing (for example "flask" and "bottle", "navy" and "dark blue"), each side drops at least one attribute, and a character-level typo rate of 2% is applied. Because both sides come from templates, a separate **human-written subset** of at least 60 items (two people writing blind to each other's text) is built and reported separately.
246: - **Photos:** a **real-photo subset** of at least 60 items, each photographed twice by different people with different angles and backgrounds; the other items have no photo. Image-based systems are evaluated on this subset.
247: - **Time and location:** the found time follows the lost time by a log-normal delay (median about 6 hours); the found location equals the true location with probability 0.6, is one level off with 0.3, and is random with 0.1. These are assumptions, and the noise ablations of 7.6 test how much the conclusions depend on them.
248: - **Ground truth:** exactly one true found report per lost report.
249: - **Query and pool:** each lost report is a query, and the candidate pool is all found reports in its split (true items plus the background reports).
250: - **Split:** 30% development (90 items) and 70% test (210 items), stratified by category, by item.
251: 
252: ### 7.2 Systems compared
253: 
254: | System | Description |
255: | --- | --- |
256: | A: keyword | BM25 over title and description |
257: | B: text embedding | Text signal only |
258: | C: image | Image signal only, on reports with photos |
259: | D: hybrid | Hand-weighted hybrid of 6.4 |
260: | E: learned fusion | Logistic regression over the signals and their missing-value indicators, trained on the development set |
261: | Ablations | Hybrid with one signal removed in turn (7.6) |
262: 
263: ### 7.3 Metrics
264: 
265: With one correct answer per query: **Recall@K** (equal to hit rate), **MRR**, **nDCG@K**, and **Precision@K** (capped at 1/K, so reported with that caveat), at K = 1, 3, 5 and 10. **Latency** at the 50th and 95th percentile, at 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000 candidates (synthetic vectors for scale), for approximate and exact search. End-to-end outcomes (verified returns, time to recovery, false claims, unclaimed rate) are operational metrics shown by the dashboard; the benchmark cannot measure them.
266: 
267: ### 7.4 Statistics
268: 
269: Confidence intervals come from a **bootstrap over queries** (1,000 resamples, fixed seed). Differences between systems use a **paired bootstrap** on the same queries. A system is called better only if the 95% interval of the difference excludes 0.
270: 
271: ### 7.5 Protocol and leakage control
272: 
273: Weights and the learned model are chosen on the **development set only**. The chosen configuration is written to a file, hashed, and **frozen**; the test set is evaluated once from that file. The tuning code has no access path to test labels, and a test enforces this. Every run records model names and versions, weights, random seed, dataset hash, git commit and hardware.
274: 
275: ### 7.6 Ablations and robustness
276: 
277: Remove each signal in turn; set 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100% of photos to missing; apply location noise (one level off) and time noise (24 hours off) to 0, 25 and 50% of the found reports. Report each with confidence intervals.
278: 
279: ### 7.7 Honest reporting
280: 
281: Write the hypotheses before the test run (**H1:** the hybrid has a higher MRR than the best single-signal baseline). Report the result whether or not it supports H1. State the limits: synthetic text and location and time rules share assumptions with the scoring function, so any advantage from location and time is partly by construction; the real-photo and human-written subsets are small; and nothing here shows real-world recovery gains.

### Starting Step 7: Multimodal Matching Engine (AC-51 to AC-67)

This step contains a **`[LEARN]`** module per `ag.md`:
> *The location and time scores, and the hybrid score with missing signals and its explanations (spec sections 6.3 to 6.6).*

#### Design & Key Edge Cases Overview:
1. **Time Score (Spec 6.3, AC-52):**
   - **Overlap:** If the lost window and found window overlap, the score is strictly **1.0**.
   - **Asymmetry:** An item cannot be found before it was lost (except for slight reporting error). Hence:
     - Found *after* lost (`gap` hours): $\text{score} = \exp(-\text{gap} / 48)$ (e.g. 12h $\to 0.7788$, 48h $\to 0.3679$).
     - Found *before* lost (`gap` hours): $\text{score} = \exp(-\text{gap} / 6)$ (steeper decay; 6h $\to 0.3679$, 12h $\to 0.1353$).
2. **Missing Signals & Renormalization (Spec 6.4, AC-53, AC-54):**
   - Default weights: Text **0.40**, Image **0.35**, Location **0.15**, Time **0.10**.
   - **Critical Rule:** Missing signals are **never treated as zero** (a report without a photo is not evidence of a non-match). Instead, weights are dynamically renormalized:
     $$\text{score} = \frac{\sum_{i \in \text{available}} w_i s_i}{\sum_{i \in \text{available}} w_i}$$
     *(e.g., when the image signal is missing, remaining weights sum to 0.65; signals 0.8, 0.7, 0.5 yield $\frac{0.475}{0.65} = 0.7308$)*.
3. **Explanations & Exact Additivity (Spec 6.6, AC-59):**
   - Signal contribution: $c_i = \frac{w_i s_i}{\sum_{j \in \text{available}} w_j}$.
   - The sum of contributions $\sum c_i$ strictly equals the combined score (within $10^{-9}$).
   - Explanations list signals contributing $\ge 10\%$ of the score in plain human language without leaking any private fields.
4. **Candidate Pruning & Tie Breaking (Spec 6.5, AC-56, AC-57):**
   - Must be `open` lost-found pairs with different reporters (`lost.reporter_id != found.reporter_id`), pair not previously dismissed, and found time within $[-6\text{h}, +30\text{d}]$ of the lost window.
   - Deterministic tie-breaking: `score DESC`, then `found.created_at ASC` (older found item first), then `found.id ASC`.

Per your standing instruction ("you write it"), I am ready to write the TDD test suite (`tests/test_ac_51_to_67_matching.py`) and implement the domain scoring, candidate retrieval, explanation generation, and `/api/reports/{id}/matches` endpoints.

+async def calculate_db_location_score(
+    db: AsyncSession, loc_a_id: uuid.UUID | None, loc_b_id: uuid.UUID | None
+) -> float | None:
+    """Calculate location similarity score between two locations in the database."""
+    if loc_a_id is None or loc_b_id is None:
+        return None
+    if loc_a_id == loc_b_id:
+        return 1.0
+
+    from sqlalchemy import select
+
+    from app.domain.location import LocationNode, calculate_location_score
+    from app.models.location import CampusLocation, LocationAdjacency
+
+    locs_res = await db.execute(select(CampusLocation))
+    all_locs = {loc.id: loc for loc in locs_res.scalars().all()}
+    if loc_a_id not in all_locs or loc_b_id not in all_locs:
+        return None
+
+    adj_res = await db.execute(select(LocationAdjacency))
+    adjacency_set = {(adj.building_a, adj.building_b) for adj in adj_res.scalars().all()}
+    for a, b in list(adjacency_set):
+        adjacency_set.add((b, a))
+
+    node_map: dict[uuid.UUID, LocationNode] = {}
+
+    def get_or_create_node(lid: uuid.UUID) -> LocationNode | None:
+        if lid in node_map:
+            return node_map[lid]
+        loc = all_locs.get(lid)
+        if loc is None:
+            return None
+        parent_node = get_or_create_node(loc.parent_id) if loc.parent_id else None
+        node = LocationNode(id=loc.id, name=loc.name, kind=loc.kind, parent=parent_node)
+        node_map[lid] = node
+        return node
+
+    node_a = get_or_create_node(loc_a_id)
+    node_b = get_or_create_node(loc_b_id)
+    return calculate_location_score(node_a, node_b, adjacency_set)

The following code has been modified to include a line number before every line, in the format: <line_number>: <original_line>. Please note that any changes targeting the original code should remove the line number, colon, and leading space.
150:     * Preference enforcement: user opt-out (`notify_matches: false`) skips match emails while preserving critical claim/handover communications.
151:     * Spam protection: hard cap of 5 match suggestion emails per user per 24-hour window.
152:   * **In-App Notification API (AC-74):**
153:     * Paginated, owner-only notification inbox (`GET /api/notifications`) with filters (`status=all|unread|read`) and stable cursor pagination.
154:     * Read receipt tracking (`POST /api/notifications/{id}/read`) with 404 anti-enumeration against other users' notifications.
155: * **Why it is designed that way:**
156:   * **Transactional Outbox Pattern:** By writing job records and notifications into PostgreSQL within the same database transaction as reports and claims, we solve the dual-write problem. If the transaction aborts, no orphaned jobs or emails are sent. If external systems (SMTP, embedding inference) are temporarily offline, the persistent queue ensures durable delivery without data loss.
157:   * **`SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`:** PostgreSQL natively coordinates concurrent workers without distributed locking (Redis, ZooKeeper). Unclaimed jobs are locked and handed to the requesting worker, while other workers skip already locked rows without waiting, achieving maximum concurrency and zero duplicates.
158:   * **Model Registry Decoupling:** Storing model names, versions, and embedding dimensions in a model registry decouples ML model lifecycle from application code. Activating a newer embedding model automatically triggers background backfilling for historical records while preserving existing vectors.
159:   * **Canonical Event Keys:** Using deterministic event keys (e.g., `match_suggested:reportA:reportB`) prevents notification floods caused by worker restarts, duplicate webhooks, or retry loops.
160: * **One thing that could go wrong:**
161:   * **Alembic Revision ID Column Width:** PostgreSQL `alembic_version.version_num` is a `VARCHAR(32)` column. Migration revision IDs exceeding 32 characters (e.g. `0006_jobs_embeddings_notifications`) trigger database-level string truncation errors. Keeping revision identifiers concise (e.g., `0006_jobs_embed_notifs`) prevents deployment failures.

+## Step 7: The Matching Engine (Signals, Hybrid, Retrieval, and Explanations)
+* **Acceptance Criteria:** AC-51 to AC-67
+* **What was built:**
+  * **Pure Domain Scoring & Candidate Logic (`app/domain/matching.py`):**
+    * Text score (AC-51): $\max(0, \text{cosine})$ of normalized embeddings (tested on cosine 0.82 $\to$ 0.82, -0.10 $\to$ 0.0).
+    * Time score (AC-52): Overlapping windows score 1.0; asymmetric exponential decay if found after lost ($\exp(-\text{gap}/48)$; 12h $\to$ 0.7788, 48h $\to$ 0.3679) and if found before lost ($\exp(-\text{gap}/6)$; 6h $\to$ 0.3679, 12h $\to$ 0.1353).
+    * Hybrid score with dynamic weight renormalization (AC-53, AC-54): Sums $\frac{\sum w_i s_i}{\sum w_i}$ strictly over non-null signals, never treating missing signals as zero (signals 0.8, 0.6, 0.7, 0.5 score 0.685; with image missing, weights renormalize over 0.65 yielding 0.7308; a text-only pair scores exactly its text score).
+    * Image signal determination (AC-55): Image-to-image similarity when both have photos, text-to-image cross-similarity when exactly one has photos, and null when neither does.
+    * Candidate constraints validation (AC-56): Both reports `open`, reporters differ, pair not dismissed, found item not reserved or returned, found time between 6 hours before lost window starts and 30 days after it ends.
+    * Deterministic tie-breaking (AC-57): Sorts by `score DESC`, then `found.created_at ASC` (older found item first), then `found.id ASC`.
+    * Explainability & Exact Additivity (AC-59): Signal contributions $c_i = \frac{w_i s_i}{\sum w_j}$ sum to the combined score within $10^{-9}$; plain language explanations for signals contributing $\ge 10\%$ of score (or top 3).
+  * **Database Infrastructure & Migrations (`0007_match_candidates.py`, `0008_hnsw_indexes.py`):**
+    * Tables `match_candidates` and `match_feedback` with unique constraint `(lost_id, found_id, weights_version)` and status indexes.
+    * pgvector HNSW vector cosine indexes (`vector_cosine_ops`) created on `text_embeddings` and `image_embeddings` for approximate nearest-neighbor search.
+  * **Matching Services & API (`services/matching.py`, `api/matches.py`):**
+    * `compute_matches_for_report`: Bidirectional candidate scoring (lost triggers found, found triggers lost), idempotent upsert, and transactional match suggestion notification creation for top 3 candidates scoring $\ge 0.65$ (AC-63, AC-65).
+    * `GET /api/reports/{id}/matches` (AC-58): Owner-only matching endpoint (404 anti-enumeration for foreign users) returning score, bin, signals, explanations, and strictly whitelisted public found item summaries (`PublicFoundItemSummary`).
+    * Privacy Canary Contract (AC-60): Canary string in private details never appears in explanations, responses, notifications, or logs.
+    * Permanent Dismissal (AC-61): `POST /api/matches/{id}/dismiss` marks candidate as dismissed, records feedback, and prevents dismissed pairs from reappearing.
+    * AI Advisory Enforcement (AC-62): Verified that artificial score updates (e.g. 0.99) never alter report or claim status.
+    * Model & Weights Versioning (AC-64): Stores `weights_version` and `model_versions`; changing weights preserves historical runs.
+    * HNSW Recall & Latency Verification (AC-66, AC-67): Verified HNSW recall@10 $\ge 90\%$ against exact flat search and retrieval/scoring latency $< 200$ ms at p50 and $< 800$ ms at p95.
+* **Why it is designed that way:**
+  * **Dynamic Weight Renormalization:** Treating missing signals (such as an absent photo) as zero would severely penalize honest reporters who lost an item for which they had no picture. Renormalizing remaining weights preserves fairness across varying signal availability.
+  * **Asymmetric Time Decay:** While an item cannot physically be found before it was lost (except for slight human reporting errors in timestamps, allowing a steep 6-hour half-decay), lost items commonly sit undetected in campus hallways or lost-and-found bins for days or weeks (represented by a gradual 48-hour decay).
+  * **Layering & Separation of Concerns:** Domain matching calculations contain zero database or framework imports, allowing the exact formulas and worked numbers from the specification to be tested with high-speed, deterministic unit tests.
+  * **AI as Advisory Only:** Under campus policy and ethical guidelines, automated similarity scores serve exclusively to surface candidate suggestions to human owners and staff, never triggering automated lifecycle or claim decisions.
+* **One thing that could go wrong:**
+  * **HNSW Index Autogenerate Drift:** Creating pgvector HNSW indexes in raw SQL without declaring them in SQLAlchemy model `__table_args__` causes `alembic check` to flag unmanaged indexes as dropped. Explicitly declaring `Index("ix_text_embeddings_hnsw", "vector", postgresql_using="hnsw", postgresql_ops={"vector": "vector_cosine_ops"})` in the model metadata keeps database state and Python schema in lockstep.
+* **Quiz Questions (for viva preparation):**
+  1. *Why must missing multimodal signals be dynamically excluded and weights renormalized rather than imputed as 0.0 in lost-and-found matching?*
+  2. *What is the mathematical justification for an asymmetric exponential decay function in the time similarity score?*
+  3. *How does the explanation generator guarantee that the sum of individual signal contributions strictly equals the combined hybrid score?*

1: # SPEC.md: Smart Campus Lost-and-Found Network
2: 
3: **Version:** 1.0 (draft, based on *Smart Campus Lost-and-Found Network: Project Blueprint*)
4: **Last updated:** 2026-10-18
5: **Methodology:** Spec-Driven Development. Every requirement has an ID, and every acceptance criterion (AC) becomes at least one automated test or one recorded measurement.
6: 
7: > Numbers marked *initial* (thresholds, weights, targets) are starting values. If you change one after measuring, record the change in the Decisions Log (section 20). The results of the evaluation are **findings**, not targets: report whichever way they fall.
8: 
9: ---
10: 
11: ## 1. Overview
12: 
13: A full-stack web application where campus users report lost and found belongings, the system suggests likely matches using text, photos, campus location and time, and campus staff verify claims and complete handovers with a one-time code. AI suggestions are **advice for humans**: no score ever approves a claim or changes a status.
14: 
15: The project has two halves of equal weight. The **product** half is a trustworthy workflow: privacy-aware public listings, evidence-based claims, moderator review, expiring single-use handover codes, an audit trail, and retention rules. The **research** half asks a measurable question: *does combining text, image, location and time signals retrieve lost items better than keyword search?* It is answered on a controlled benchmark with proper splits, confidence intervals and ablations.
16: 
17: The blueprint itself notes that AI-assisted lost-and-found systems already exist. This project does not claim a novel idea. Its contribution is a careful, secure, explainable campus workflow and an honestly measured comparison.
18: 
19: ### Aim
20: 
21: Build a secure, campus-aware lost-and-found platform with explainable multimodal matching, a verified claim and handover process, and a reproducible evaluation of hybrid retrieval against keyword and single-signal baselines, deployed as a service you can open in a browser on your computer or local network.
22: 
23: ### Inputs
24: 
25: | Input | Details |
26: | --- | --- |
27: | Accounts | Campus email, password, display name (optional) |
28: | Reports | Lost or found: title, description, category, time (with precision), campus location (any level), up to 3 photos, optional private details and verification prompts (found reports) |
29: | Claims | Evidence text, answers to verification prompts, up to 3 private evidence photos |
30: | Moderator actions | Approve or remove reports, decide claims, issue and verify handover codes |
31: | Campus data | A location tree and building adjacency, maintained by admins |
32: | Models | A pinned text-embedding model and a pinned image-text model (section 6.1) |
33: | Benchmark data | A synthetic generator plus a small real-photo subset, with a data card (section 7) |
34: | Configuration | Environment variables: database URL, secrets, allowed email domains, SMTP, retention periods, model versions |
35: 
36: ### Outputs
37: 
38: | Output | Details |
39: | --- | --- |
40: | Searchable listings | Found items visible to authenticated campus users, without private details |
41: | Ranked match suggestions | Top candidates for each report, with a score, a bin and a plain-language explanation |
42: | Claims and handovers | Reviewed claims, expiring handover codes, completed returns with an audit trail |
43: | Notifications | In-app and email, with no private details |
44: | Analytics | Recovery rate, time to recovery, unclaimed rate, volume and queue age |
45: | Evaluation results | Tables and plots of retrieval quality, ablations and latency, with confidence intervals and recorded model versions |
46: | Deployed service | The web application, running in containers at `http://localhost:8080` (and over HTTPS on the local network) |
47: 
48: ### Requirements at a glance
49:

56: ## 2. Goals, Scope and Non-Goals
57: 
58: **Goals**
59: 1. Accounts with roles (user, moderator, admin) and campus-email verification.
60: 2. A hierarchical campus location model that tolerates approximate locations.
61: 3. Lost and found reports with a safe photo pipeline and a defined lifecycle.
62: 4. Searchable listings that never expose private details.
63: 5. Background embedding jobs and a hybrid matching engine with explanations.
64: 6. Notifications (in-app and email) through a reliable outbox.
65: 7. Claims, moderator review, and one-time handover codes.
66: 8. An append-only audit log, retention rules, and data export and deletion.
67: 9. An analytics dashboard.
68: 10. A reproducible evaluation of keyword, text, image and hybrid retrieval.
69: 11. A tested, documented, deployed system.
70: 
71: **Non-goals (v1)**
72: - Campus single sign-on, mobile apps, push notifications, or SMS.
73: - Automatic ownership decisions, or any AI action without human review.
74: - GPS tracking or precise indoor positioning.
75: - Facial recognition. Photos are never used to identify people.
76: - Evidence that the system improves real-world recovery rates (only a pilot could show that; the benchmark does not).
77: 
78: **Stretch** (only after every required criterion passes): a SigLIP-family model comparison, multilingual text, face and number-plate blurring in photos, learning from dismissals, campus SSO, and a digest email.
